hints: Look at what changes from ethanol to ethanoic acid, a primary alcohol is fully oxidised past the aldehyde stage, so think which strong oxidiser does this.
Think about the conditions needed to keep the volatile aldehyde intermediate in the flask so it can be oxidised a second time.
walkthrough:
Spot the level of oxidation**
You start with $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}$, a primary alcohol, and you finish with $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$, a carboxylic acid. That is full oxidation, it must go through ethanal first and then on to the acid. Only a strong oxidising agent can do both steps.

Name the classic AS oxidiser**
For alcohols the standard strong oxidiser is dichromate(VI) in acid. Write acidified $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ or $\text{Na}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$. Acidified is essential, the $\text{H}^+$ is needed for the half equation.

Choose reflux to get the acid**
If you gently distil you collect ethanal and stop there. To force the second oxidation to the acid you heat under reflux, so any ethanal condenses and drops back into the hot oxidising mixture until reaction is complete.

Final answer: reagent(s): acidified potassium dichromate(VI), $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ (or sodium dichromate, $\text{Na}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$)
conditions: heat under reflux

hints: Count atoms on each side using $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}$ to $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{H}$, then work out how many [O] and how many $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ balance O and H.
walkthrough:
Balance with [O] as the oxidiser**
Write the carbon skeleton first: $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}$ to $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{H}$. You need two extra O atoms on the left to make the two O atoms in the $\text{COOH}$ group, so use $2[\text{O}]$. Then balance H by adding $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ on the right: $$\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH} + 2[\text{O}] \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{H} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$ Check: C 2 to 2, H 6 to 6, O 3 to 3.

hints: Compare $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ with $\text{BrCH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$, one H on the methyl group is swapped for Br, so what general type replaces one atom by another?
walkthrough:
See what is swapped**
In reaction 2, $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ becomes $\text{BrCH}_2\text{COOH}$. The carbon skeleton is unchanged, one $\text{C-H}$ bond on the methyl group becomes a $\text{C-Br}$ bond. When an atom is exchanged for another with no other major change, that is substitution.

hints: Think what homo means, same, and recall that in reaction 3 the acid, alcohol and $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ are all mixed together in one liquid phase.
walkthrough:
Remember the meaning of homogeneous**
Homogeneous catalyst means the catalyst and the reactants are in one single phase. Here reaction 3 is esterification in solution, the concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ dissolves in the same liquid mixture as the carboxylic acid and ethanol, so it is homogeneous, not on a separate solid surface.
Final answer: Because $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ is in the same phase / same state as the reactants

hints: Start from the fruity smell of B and the fact that D forms from C plus ethanol like an esterification, what functional group links an acid and an alcohol?
Use the Data Booklet values to match the two strong peaks at $1100 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ and $1720 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ to specific bonds.
Think why the absence of any O-H absorption is powerful evidence, what two O-H containing groups in C must have disappeared to form D?
walkthrough:
Predict from chemistry**
C is $\text{HOCH}_2\text{COOH}$, it has both a carboxylic acid and an alcohol group. With ethanol and $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ in reaction 3 it can esterify. D is said to have two identical functional groups, which fits a diester type product formed when both acid and alcohol ends react.

Match the two key IR peaks**
Check the Data Booklet. A strong peak at $1720 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ is the classic $\text{C=O}$ stretch of an ester (and acids too), and a strong peak at $1100 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ is the $\text{C-O}$ stretch of an ester. Having both together points strongly to ester.

Use the missing peak**
Crucially there is no $\text{O-H}$ absorption. C would show broad $\text{O-H}$ for $\text{COOH}$ around $2500$ to $3000 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ and $\text{O-H}$ for alcohol around $3200$ to $3600 \text{ cm}^{-1}$. Their absence in D tells you both the $\text{COOH}$ and the alcoholic $\text{OH}$ have been consumed to make ester links, confirming D contains ester groups and no free acid or alcohol.

Final answer: Functional group in D: ester
$1100 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ due to $\text{C-O}$ and $1720 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ due to $\text{C=O}$
No absorption due to $\text{O-H}$, so no $\text{COOH}$ and no alcohol $\text{OH}$ remain in D, the $\text{COOH}$ and $\text{OH}$ groups of C have reacted / been lost.

hints: Recall that only the acidic $\text{COOH}$ proton reacts with $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$, the neutral alcohol $\text{OH}$ is untouched, so what sodium salt forms from $\text{HOCH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$?
walkthrough:
React the acid end only**
C is $\text{HOCH}_2\text{COOH}$. Carbonate neutralises carboxylic acids but not alcohols. So the $\text{COOH}$ loses $\text{H}^+$ to give $\text{COO}^-\text{Na}^+$, while $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ stays as it is. E is therefore sodium 2-hydroxyethanoate, $\text{HOCH}_2\text{COO}^-\text{Na}^+$.

hints: Think about what $\text{NaBH}_4$ can and cannot reduce at AS level, it reduces aldehydes and ketones but what about the very stable $\text{COOH}$ group?
walkthrough:
Compare reducing power**
To make F, $\text{(CH}_2\text{OH)}_2$, you must reduce the $\text{COOH}$ group of C to $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$. $\text{NaBH}_4$ is a mild reducing agent, good for aldehydes and ketones, but it is not strong enough to reduce a carboxylic acid. You would need the stronger $\text{LiAlH}_4$ for that change.
Final answer: $\text{NaBH}_4$ is not a strong enough reducing agent (to reduce the carboxylic acid in C)

hints: Treat $(\text{CH}_2\text{OH})_2$ as the diol reactant and $\text{SOCl}_2$ as the chlorinating agent giving $(\text{CH}_2\text{Cl})_2$, then add the usual $\text{SO}_2$ and water type by-products as given in the scheme.
walkthrough:
Write the chlorination equation**
$\text{SOCl}_2$ replaces alcoholic $\text{OH}$ by $\text{Cl}$. Here the diol $(\text{CH}_2\text{OH})_2$ becomes the dichloride $(\text{CH}_2\text{Cl})_2$. Construct the equation as required: $$(\text{CH}_2\text{OH})_2 + \text{SOCl}_2 \rightarrow (\text{CH}_2\text{Cl})_2 + \text{SO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

hints: Look at the two polar groups in C, $\text{OH}$ and $\text{COOH}$, and think what specific strong attraction they can form with water molecules.
walkthrough:
Link polar groups to water**
C, $\text{HOCH}_2\text{COOH}$, is small and has two very polar groups, an alcohol $\text{OH}$ and a carboxylic acid $\text{COOH}$. Both contain $\text{O-H}$ and $\text{C=O}$ that can hydrogen bond to water molecules. These solute to water hydrogen bonds replace water to water bonds, releasing enough energy to dissolve the molecule very readily.
Final answer: C forms hydrogen bonds with water
